items.title: [abc.net.au] Lancet researchers urge health emergency declaration as climate losses mount
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heat-related disruption cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost worker productivity in 2025, while extreme drought affected about 52% of global land for at least a month, according to the 2026 Lancet Countdown report. The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

Oklahoma will prohibit data centers from using groundwater for evaporative cooling starting Nov. 1, requiring closed-loop or immersion systems under a new law. The restriction applies to water use inside facilities, but electricity generation can account for a larger share of data centers’ water footprint. The law follows drought conditions in western Oklahoma during much of 2026; Pennsylvania has separately required data centers using more than 10 megawatts to disclose energy and water use. Forbes cited national figures showing that power plants serving data centers consumed far more water in 2023 than data centers used for cooling.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Swedish survey finds valuable meadows stable, but upkeep remains essential
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Sweden’s valuable meadows and grazing lands have largely retained their natural and cultural value, according to an analysis by the Swedish Board of Agriculture. Of 300,000 hectares identified as valuable, 260,000 had been fully inventoried. In 2020, nearly 70% of that fully inventoried area — 175,000 hectares — received environmental management payments, 8,000 hectares more than in 2018. Repeat surveys conducted 10 to 20 years apart found that most inventoried sites remained meadows or pastures. Some sites lost value when left unmanaged and became overgrown, while restoration helped recover value elsewhere. The agency says continued inventories are needed to track changes.

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] This Tiny Meshtastic Node Is Solar Ready: Base Uno First Look
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Muzi Works Base Uno caught my attention because it packs quite a few useful features into a very small Meshtastic board. It comes pre-flashed, includes a 1,500 mAh battery, and has dedicated connections for a solar panel. That is a pretty interesting starting point for a little off-grid node. I bought the kit to find out how easily it would get going and whether the solar input actually worked. By the end of my first round of testing, it had connected over Bluetooth, discovered nearby nodes, completed a traceroute, and charged its battery to around 96% using a small solar panel. So far, this little board is looking good. Key Takeaways The Base Uno kit includes a pre-flashed Meshtastic board, antenna, and 1,500 mAh three-wire LiPo battery. Bluetooth pairing worked with PIN 123456, and I retained Long Fast to match my existing mesh. A small solar panel connected to PV+ and ground raised the reported battery level to about 96%. The app eventually showed 33 online nodes, and a traceroute to a node roughly a mile away succeeded. Table of Contents What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh Node Discovery Took a Little Patience Connecting a Small Solar Panel More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? What Comes in the Base Uno Kit? The kit includes the essentials for getting the board powered up and connected: The Base Uno board, carrying Elecrow and Muzi Works branding. A small screw-on antenna. A USB cable. A 1,500 mAh rechargeable LiPo battery. A small Allen key and screws. The board itself is quite compact. There is a reset button and a user button, but no display. Configuration and status checks happen through the Meshtastic app rather than on a screen attached to the node. Its nRF processor is one reason I was interested in it. This is the sort of hardware I would expect to be light on battery use, which makes it appealing for both a portable device and a solar-powered installation. I have not measured its power consumption or battery runtime yet, though, so those remain things to test rather than results from this first look. The Three-Wire Battery Is an Interesting Detail The included battery stood out more than I expected. It is a 1,500 mAh LiPo with three wires, rather than just the usual positive and negative leads. The third wire is a sensing connection. My understanding is that it provides battery temperature information that the charging circuitry can use to manage charging, including stopping it when conditions are unsuitable. That is particularly interesting on a board intended for solar use. I like seeing that extra sensing connection, but I did not test the temperature cutoff or establish its operating thresholds. The important distinction here is that the battery offers more than a simple two-wire power connection. Confirming exactly how the board responds to that sensing input will need further testing. Hardware Connections for Expansion and Solar There is quite a bit available around the edges of this little board: QWIIC port: An expansion connection I plan to try in a separate test. SDA and SCL pins: The labeled I2C connections. TX and RX pins: Serial connections for additional projects. OLED-related connections: Useful options if a display becomes part of the build. PV+ and ground: The dedicated solar-panel connections. Battery connector: Located on the back of the board, separate from the QWIIC port. That last distinction is worth paying attention to during assembly. The battery does not plug into the QWIIC port. I checked the connector location and orientation before seating it in the battery socket on the back. The PV+ and ground connections are what make this especially tempting as a solar-node project. Rather than starting with a separate charging arrangement, there is already a place on the board to bring in the panel. First Power-Up and Bluetooth Pairing Connect the antenna before powering up the node. I screwed on the supplied antenna first, then connected the battery. An LED came on straight away, which was a good start. The package identified the board as pre-flashed with Meshtastic, so there was no initial firmware installation to work through. My setup sequence was straightforward: Attach the antenna. Plug the battery into the correct battery connector. Open the Meshtastic app and look for the node over Bluetooth. Select the discovered Meshtastic device. Enter the Bluetooth pairing PIN. Allow the app to load the node information. Because there is no display, I tried the default PIN, 123456, and it connected successfully. The Bluetooth settings later confirmed that this was the configured PIN. It can be changed there rather than left at the default. My unit arrived running Meshtastic 2.7.15. The app initially reported the battery at 45%, while a later device-metrics reading showed 67%. Those were the reported values during setup, not a controlled battery-capacity measurement. Changing the Node Name I went into the user settings and gave the node a recognizable name using my vervesoft.live naming scheme with a Muzi identifier. Saving the change caused the node to reboot. The Bluetooth connection dropped while it restarted, and the status LED changed colors before the node returned. The same behavior occurred when saving the LoRa settings. A brief disconnect after saving was part of the restart, not a failed setup. Configuring LoRa to Match the Local Mesh The board initially had the Long Fast modem preset selected. My other nodes were still using Long Fast, so I kept this board on the same settings for the first test. Selecting the US region in the app changed the preset to Long Turbo during this setup. I changed it back to Long Fast so the Base Uno would match my existing nodes. These were the US-region combinations shown during the test: Long Fast: Frequency slot 20, operating at 906.875 MHz. Long Turbo: Frequency slot 14, operating at 908.75 MHz. Long Turbo was the newer default I encountered at the time, but compatibility with the mesh I already had running was the immediate priority. There was no point leaving this one node on a different preset while the rest were still waiting to be migrated. Choose the correct region for your location and check that the radio settings match the nodes you intend to use. The US settings above describe this particular setup, not a configuration to copy regardless of country. Other Settings I Checked With the radio configured, I worked through the remaining settings: Channels: A Long Fast channel was already present. Position sharing: The installed firmware allowed it on that channel, with an approximately 1.8-mile position-precision radius shown. Device role: The board was set to Client. Time zone: I used the computer’s time zone. Buzzer: The configuration listed pin 22, although I did not add or test a buzzer. Display: Display settings were turned off. Bluetooth: The fixed PIN was set to 123456. There was no GPS installed on this setup, so the position-sharing option did not mean the board was producing its own GPS location. It also had no environmental readings available. Node Discovery Took a Little Patience At first, the node list stayed empty apart from the Base Uno itself. I enabled the option to include unknown nodes, but there was still nothing else immediately. I expected it to find somebody fairly quickly. Instead of changing everything at once, I left it running and checked a few diagnostics. The signal-quality page did not provide a noise-floor reading with the installed firmware. It did show transmit and receive counters, including one TX and one RX at that stage. Battery telemetry was available, but there was no environmental or position data. Then another node appeared, identified as 49D4. That was the first useful confirmation that the Base Uno was receiving another mesh node. More entries followed as it continued running. The practical lesson from this first startup was simple: an empty node list in the first few minutes did not turn out to mean the board was faulty. In this case, it needed a little time. I also checked the firmware version against the releases available at the time. The unit had 2.7.15, while 2.7.26 was listed as the latest stable release then. I left the firmware alone for this test so I could establish how the kit behaved as supplied. Connecting a Small Solar Panel Once the basic setup was working, I tried the feature that interested me most: solar charging. I took a small panel described as roughly 200 mA and soldered its leads to the PV+ and ground connections on the back of the board. The LiPo battery remained connected, and I placed the assembly outside for a short test. The first solar test used a small panel connected directly to the board’s dedicated solar input. This was a bare-board experiment, not a finished outdoor installation. I still need to find a suitable case before turning it into a permanent node. Solar Charging Results There was a useful amount of sun, followed by some cloud, so the panel did not have uninterrupted sunshine throughout the test. Even so, the reported battery level rose from readings in the 60% to 70% range earlier in the session to approximately 95% to 96%. The device-metrics graph showed the upward charging trend after the assembly had been outside. That is the encouraging result: the solar input worked, and the reported battery charge increased while the node was operating. This was not a measured charging-efficiency test, and it does not yet establish whether this particular panel can sustain the node through nights and poor weather. It does show that the basic solar-charging arrangement is functional. More Nodes and a Successful Traceroute After the board had been running outside for a while, the app showed 33 online nodes with unknown entries filtered out. That was quite a change from the nearly empty list during the first few minutes. I then requested a traceroute to another node, and it returned successfully. The other node was roughly a mile down the road, which was a pleasing result with the little supplied stubby antenna still attached. I would not turn that into a maximum-range claim. This was an initial connectivity check, not a controlled range test. Still, the board was doing the things I wanted to establish first: receiving mesh traffic and completing a traceroute. A Mobile Node or a Permanent Solar Node? That is now the interesting decision. The Base Uno is small enough to make a neat portable build, but the dedicated solar input makes a permanent solar node very tempting. For a mobile build, the compact board and included 1,500 mAh battery are appealing. For a solar build, the working panel input and three-wire battery sensing are the details that stand out. My next steps are to find a case, update the firmware, and test the QWIIC port. I also want more time with the power system before making any claims about long-term autonomy. For now, this is a very positive first impression. It booted, paired, accepted configuration changes, discovered nearby nodes, and charged from a small solar panel. That is a pretty good start for a tiny Meshtastic board. Affiliate disclosure: I may earn from qualifying purchases through the product link below. items.title: [farms.com] Livestock reports highlight forage planning amid drought and feed-supply concerns
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Livestock guidance published across the United States, France and Poland focuses on forage stocks, grazing and feed transitions during drought and uneven feed supplies. In France, independent livestock nutrition consultant Eva Garre urged farmers to measure silage and hay reserves, account for losses of 15% to 30% and calculate shortages by date; early maize samples showed starch levels of 18 to 20 points, compared with the usual 34 to 37 in her region. Kenny Simon, an extension forages instructor at the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, recommended rotational grazing, moving hay-feeding sites and planting winter annuals to reduce stress on dry pastures. A Polish cattle farm keeps cows and calves on about 100 hectares of pasture from May through November and produces its own hay and silage. South Dakota State University Extension feedlot specialist Warren Rusche advised keeping newly arrived calves in smaller feedlot pens for their first three weeks and feeding them twice daily during the initial adjustment. Argentine feedlot analyst Andrés Halle cautioned that theoretical feedlot margins can misstate results when current grain prices are applied to grain produced on-farm.

items.title: [climatechangenews.com] Brazil sets voluntary timetable for global shift from fossil fuels
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Brazil’s presidency of the COP30 climate summit published a 182-page voluntary roadmap on Nov. 3 to help countries move away from coal, oil and gas, proposing a staged process through 2033. It asks governments to prepare national plans by 2028, build clean-energy systems and supporting infrastructure through 2030, then focus on adjusting fossil-fuel supply from 2031 to 2033. The guide does not assign obligations to individual countries or set binding phaseout targets; it offers a framework for governments to assess their circumstances and choose measures. Brazil says it is meant to help governments implement existing climate agreements. COP31 opens in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9, and the roadmap is scheduled for discussion there on Nov. 10.

items.title: [downtoearth.org.in] Cyclone Arnab stalls off India, prolonging rain and flood threat
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Cyclone Arnab’s slow, near-stationary approach to India’s Andhra Pradesh coast prolonged the landfall process and heightened the risk of extreme rain and flash flooding, Down To Earth reported. The storm crossed the southeastern coast on Wednesday, Oct. 28, after forming over the Bay of Bengal. Greenland’s parliament voted 16-0 on Nov. 3, with seven lawmakers abstaining, to approve a security agreement with Denmark and the United States, clearing the way for expanded U.S. military access to the Arctic island. The pact permits two new U.S. defense sites and supports the Golden Dome missile-defense system while affirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. It would remain in force if Greenland later becomes independent. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the agreement in September after Trump repeatedly pressed for U.S. control of Greenland and threatened force and tariffs against allies. Denmark has rejected a transfer of the territory but had been open to discussing a larger U.S. military presence. The Danish parliament is scheduled to take up the measure on Nov. 11 and vote on Nov. 19. The pact takes effect after the required Danish and Greenlandic parliamentary procedures and does not require U.S. Senate approval. Greenlandic officials and residents remain divided over whether the security arrangement brings tangible benefits to the island.

items.title: [nasa.gov] 4.1-billion-year-old Mars meteorite reveals evidence of ancient water
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA-funded researchers say Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali’s Sahara in 2022, formed in Mars’ crust at least 4.1 billion years ago, potentially making it the oldest of about 435 Martian meteorites identified on Earth. The study, published in Science on Oct. 29, describes a rare sample from the planet’s early crust; only three known Martian meteorites date to that period. The rock is a coarse-grained igneous material called gabbro, formed as magma cooled underground. Its oxygen and hydrogen isotope signatures, along with altered minerals, indicate that water reached deep into the crust and interacted with rock more than 4.1 billion years ago; the rock itself likely formed earlier. Spacecraft observations have also shown evidence of ancient water on Mars. Researchers say the evidence supports the possibility that early Mars had habitable conditions, but does not show that life existed there. Orbital mineral data point to 13 possible source locations in the planet’s southern highlands, but the meteorite’s precise birthplace remains unknown.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.title: [aljazeera.com] Trump says no immediate Iran strikes planned as Hormuz talks stall
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

President Donald Trump said the United States has no immediate plans for further strikes on Iran, though he confirmed a limited U.S. attack on Qeshm Island and left open the possibility of more action. The eight-month conflict between Washington and Tehran is also threatening shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route at the center of indirect negotiations. Trump told the Financial Times the United States was “getting everything” it wanted and said American forces were ready to act if needed. He said the Qeshm strike hit a newly completed Iranian anti-aircraft facility; U.S. officials described it as a limited defensive operation, not a return to major combat. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, called Washington’s response to Tehran’s seven conditions unconvincing. Iran has tied reopening Hormuz to conditions including lifting sanctions, ending the U.S. naval blockade and releasing frozen funds. Qatar says both sides are reviewing proposals, but a senior Iranian official told Reuters they remain far from a deal. Two projectiles also hit a tanker off Oman on Tuesday; no injuries or environmental damage were reported.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Random draw makes Jennifer Thoss Lytton’s mayor after 45-45 tie
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Jennifer Thoss will become mayor of Lytton, British Columbia, after a random draw broke a 45-45 tie with incumbent Denise O’Connor in the Oct. 17 election. A judicial recount at Kamloops Provincial Court on Tuesday confirmed the tally before the draw selected Thoss. Thoss will lead a village rebuilding after a 2021 wildfire that killed two people and destroyed most of its structures. A former councillor, she has criticized the pace of recovery and warned that more than $50 million in planned infrastructure could overwhelm Lytton’s reduced tax base. O’Connor defended the need for recovery staff and infrastructure to attract residents. Thoss said after the draw that she would focus on team-building.
